groups.high: UNCLOS Article 98 requires a flag State to impose duties of assistance on the master of a ship flying its flag, subject to the master being able to act without serious danger to the ship, crew, or passengers. The duties include assisting anyone found at sea in danger of being lost and proceeding with all possible speed to rescue persons in distress when informed of their need, so far as such action may reasonably be expected. A MAYDAY call can communicate that need, but assistance is not legally dependent on hearing that exact word. Nationality or migration status is not a reason to disregard human life at sea. However, the treaty does not create an unconditional obligation for every nearby ship or aircraft to attempt an impossible rescue regardless of serious danger. Article 98 also addresses assistance following collision, subject to the same safety qualification, and obliges coastal States to promote adequate search-and-rescue services and regional cooperation where appropriate. SOLAS and the maritime search-and-rescue framework supply related duties and coordination; Article 98 is not itself a universal criminal jurisdiction provision. Masters should assess the situation and capabilities, contact the relevant rescue coordination service, and provide the assistance reasonably possible without creating serious danger. Record relevant communications and reasons for decisions. Verification should support coordination, not become a pretext to delay aid until every uncertainty is eliminated. Enforcement and particular penalties depend on the applicable implementing law, not an automatic treaty sentence.

Help must be possible without serious danger to the ship, crew, or passengers. Help anyone found at sea in danger of being lost. If told people need rescue, go with all possible speed. Do so as far as this can reasonably be expected. A MAYDAY call can show that need. The duty does not depend on hearing that exact word. Nationality is not a reason to ignore life at sea. Nor is migration status. But the rule does not demand an impossible rescue. It does not demand serious danger to the rescuing ship. It does not treat every aircraft as a ship. Article 98 also covers help after a collision. The same safety limit applies. Coastal States must promote adequate search-and-rescue services. They must cooperate regionally where appropriate. SOLAS and maritime rescue rules add duties. They help coordinate the response. Article 98 does not itself give every State power to try every crime. Assess the danger. Check what the ship can do. Contact the relevant rescue coordination service. Give the help reasonably possible without serious danger. Keep messages and reasons for decisions. Checking a call should help rescue. It should not delay aid until all doubt is gone. The law that puts the duty into effect sets penalties.

groups.high: SOLAS Chapter III, Regulation 21 distinguishes passenger-ship survival-craft arrangements by voyage and approved configuration. For passenger ships on international voyages other than short international voyages, the standard arrangement provides enclosed or partially enclosed lifeboat capacity on each side for at least fifty percent of all persons aboard. Additional liferafts provide at least twenty-five percent. Thus an illustrative ship with 1,000 persons would ordinarily have 500 lifeboat places on each side plus 250 additional raft places. The Administration may permit substitution of lifeboats with equivalent raft capacity, but the relevant arrangement retains lifeboat capacity on each side for at least 37.5 percent of all persons. Short-international-voyage ships meeting the specified subdivision standards have a different arrangement, including a thirty-percent lifeboat component, with rafts completing the baseline capacity and the additional raft provision. Small passenger ships and other specified configurations can have distinct approved requirements. Consequently, one should not state that every passenger ship has exactly the same 100-percent-lifeboat-plus-25-percent-raft configuration. All persons includes crew as well as passengers. Capacity, approved distribution, accessibility, maintenance, launching arrangements, and training all matter; nominal seats alone do not guarantee safe evacuation. An extra twenty-five percent of raft places does not prove that everyone can be accommodated after all lifeboats are lost. The source does not establish a universal twenty-four-hour lifeboat survival limit. Check the current applicable SOLAS provisions, voyage category, flag-State approval, and ship-specific life-saving plan rather than treating a simplified percentage as the complete rule.
groups.mid: SOLAS Chapter III, Regulation 21 sets passenger-ship survival-craft rules. The voyage and approved setup matter. Take an international voyage that is not a short international voyage. The standard arrangement has lifeboats on each side. Each side has places for at least half of everyone aboard. It adds liferafts for at least another quarter. For 1,000 people, that means 500 lifeboat places on each side and 250 extra raft places. The Administration may allow some boats to be replaced. The rafts must have equal capacity. In that arrangement, each side must still have lifeboat places for at least 37.5 percent of everyone aboard. Short international voyages can have different rules. The ship must meet the specified subdivision standards. There can be a thirty-percent lifeboat part, with rafts completing the baseline capacity and extra raft places added. Small ships and other specified setups can have distinct approved rules. So not every passenger ship uses exactly the same 100-percent-boat-plus-25-percent-raft setup. Everyone aboard includes crew, not just passengers. Capacity and approved placement matter. So do access, maintenance, launching, and training. A seat count alone does not ensure safe escape. An extra quarter of raft places is not enough for everyone if all boats are lost. Nor does the source give a universal twenty-four-hour survival limit for a lifeboat. Check current SOLAS rules, voyage type, flag-State approval, and the ship's life-saving plan.

groups.high: Cabin pressure altitude is the altitude in the standard atmosphere corresponding to the cabin's pressure, not the aircraft's physical altitude. Under the checked 2024 text of FAA 14 CFR 25.841, occupied pressurized cabins must normally provide a pressure altitude not exceeding 8,000 feet, with specified provisions for operations at high-elevation airports. For certification above 25,000 feet, probable pressurization failures have a 15,000-foot cabin-altitude design criterion, subject to the stated airport exception. After decompression from failures not shown extremely improbable, occupants must not be exposed above 25,000 feet for more than two minutes or above 40,000 feet for any duration. These are certification requirements, not promises that any pressure failure leaves the cabin below 8,000 feet or requires maintaining 10,000 feet for thirty minutes. The regulation also addresses controls, valves, indicators, and warnings. Physiological danger arises because reduced pressure lowers available oxygen partial pressure. FAA educational tables give roughly fifteen to twenty seconds of useful consciousness at 40,000 feet; useful task performance can fail before complete unconsciousness, the interval varies, and rapid decompression can shorten it. It is not a guaranteed safe waiting period, an irreversible-brain-injury countdown, or a reason for emergency egress at cruising altitude. Use emergency oxygen immediately as instructed and follow crew procedures; a mask bag need not inflate to deliver oxygen. Aircraft descent and pressurization response are crew tasks. Distinguish the regulatory design limits from individual physiology and the aircraft's approved operating procedures.

After decompression from failures not shown extremely improbable, exposure above 25,000 feet must not exceed two minutes. Exposure above 40,000 feet is not allowed for any duration. These are design rules. They do not promise every pressure failure stays below 8,000 feet. They do not require 10,000 feet for thirty minutes. The rule also covers valves, controls, indicators, and warnings. Thin air lowers the oxygen partial pressure available to your body. FAA learning tables give about fifteen to twenty seconds of useful consciousness at 40,000 feet. That means time to perform useful tasks, not a guaranteed time before passing out. It varies, and rapid decompression can shorten it. It is not safe time to wait or a fixed countdown to permanent brain damage. It is not a reason to leave a plane at cruise height. Use emergency oxygen at once as instructed. Follow the crew. A mask bag need not inflate for oxygen to flow. The crew handles descent and pressure procedures. Keep design rules, body limits, and the plane's approved procedures distinct.

groups.high: For ordinary passenger carriage, spare lithium-ion batteries belong in cabin baggage with terminals individually protected against short circuit, not in checked baggage. The 100 Wh threshold is not an absolute ban on every larger spare: IATA guidance permits the over-100-to-160 Wh category subject to airline approval and the applicable quantity limits, commonly at most two such spares per person. Above 160 Wh is generally outside ordinary passenger-baggage allowance; specified mobility-aid and medical provisions require separate checking. A power bank is treated as a spare battery, but additional current power-bank restrictions and airline rules must also be checked rather than assuming all spare-battery allowances transfer unchanged. Read the watt-hour label and confirm approval before travel. Watt-hours express stored energy: where appropriate, Wh equals nominal volts multiplied by ampere-hours, with milliampere-hours divided by 1,000 first. Use the battery's correct nominal voltage, not an arbitrary charger output. Keep spares in original protective packaging or individually insulate terminals and use a protective pouch or case so metal objects cannot bridge them. Remove spares if hand baggage is gate-checked. Do not travel with damaged or swollen batteries; alert crew promptly to heat, smoke, or damage and follow their instructions. A short circuit can generate heat and trigger thermal runaway, a self-heating failure that can cause fire. A prohibited baggage item is not automatically acceptable as air cargo: cargo has separate classification, packing, testing, documentation, and aircraft restrictions. Confirm the actual airline and route rules.

Do not bring swollen or damaged batteries. Tell crew promptly about heat, smoke, or damage. Follow their instructions. A short circuit can cause heat and thermal runaway, a self-heating failure that may start a fire. Cargo is not an automatic alternative for a banned bag item. Cargo has separate packing, testing, documents, classification, and aircraft rules. Check your airline and route.

groups.high: Under WHO's International Health Regulations (2005), Annex 7 as amended, an International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis for yellow fever becomes valid ten days after vaccination with an approved vaccine and remains valid for the life of the vaccinated person. The lifetime amendment took effect on 11 July 2016 and applies to existing certificates as well as new ones, including older certificates showing a ten-year expiry date. A new booster or alteration of the certificate is not required to create lifetime validity; changes or erasures can compromise a certificate. This border-document rule should be distinguished from individualized medical advice, including whether vaccination is appropriate or an additional dose is advised for a particular patient. Countries may require yellow-fever vaccination proof in the circumstances covered by the IHR, but the actual destination and transit requirements must be checked for the itinerary; there is no single twelve-hour or twenty-four-hour transit rule for every country. The certificate records vaccination details, clinician signature and professional status, manufacturer and batch number, and the administering centre's official stamp in the prescribed format. A unique QR code is not a universal requirement established by Annex 7. Obtain documentation from an authorized vaccination centre, allow the ten-day validity period for a primary vaccination, and verify current entry conditions before travel. A medical contraindication or missing certificate requires destination-specific assessment of applicable IHR procedures, not a promise of universal exemption or automatic admission. Keep the certificate safe and do not modify it to rewrite an old expiry date.
